newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia capital mostly quiet in wake of clashes.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia capital mostly quiet in wake of clashes.

text.p: Indonesia's violence-marred campaign for May 29 general elections resumed on a quieter note on Wednesday, with only one report of an isolated clash between students and supporters of the ruling Golkar party in Jakarta.
Witnesses said some 2,000 students of the IAIN Islamic University on the southern outskirts of Jakarta threw stones at Golkar supporters just outside the campus.
The students retreated into the campus after marine commandos and riot police arrived and charged them with batons.

Students later gathered on the side of the road to jeer carloads of Golkar supporters, but few passed as Golkar's Jakarta branch cancelled most of its planned local meetings in south and east Jakarta.
There were no serious injuries or arrests in the incident, and police said the capital was quiet and safe in all sectors.
In Pekalongan in central Java, the scene of serious clashes on Tuesday, witnesses said PPP supporters attacked a public bus carrying Golkar supporters among its passengers on Wednesday.
Windows were smashed and the bus was overturned, witnesses said, but there were no reports of injuries or arrests. The town was otherwise calm in the face of heavy security patrols.
Widespread violence broke out across the country's main Java island in the past few days as the campaign headed into the home stretch.
Authorities have blamed a left-wing group outside the country's rigid political system for the clashes.
However, analysts and diplomats blamed the violence on increasing disparities between the rich and the poor and frustration with the country's economic and political system.
The election campaign ends on Friday, giving a cooling off period before the country's 125 million eligible voters go to the polls on Thursday of next week.
Golkar, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), and the badly-split Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) are the only parties legally permitted to contest the elections.
Golkar, in power for the last 30 years, is seeking to boost its support to more than 70 percent of the vote from 68 percent in the last elections in 1992.
Its main challenge is coming from the PPP, which political analysts say is also drawing support from one wing of the PDI and from people disillusioned with the government.
The Australian, U.S. and British embassies advised their citizens in Jakarta to be on guard against further violence.
Thursday is a national holiday, and little trouble was expected with the fractured PDI campaigning on Java.
Friday, however, could see more street violence with the PPP on the hustings in Java, which has 60 percent of Indonesia's 200 million population.

Lieutenant-General Syarwan Hamid, head of the military's socio-political section, was quoted by the official Antara news agency on Wednesday as blaming the illegal leftist People's Democratic Party (PRD) for the campaign disturbances.
"I have come to the conclusion we must suspect the PRD as being behind the acts of violence," Hamid told a closed-door meeting of media editors on Tuesday.

The Republika newspaper reported on Wednesday that Adam Khaeruddin, 20, was fatally shot while watching disturbances in the Warung Buncit area of south Jakarta on Tuesday. It did not say who shot him, but witnesses said both police and troops fired into the air to disperse a few thousand PPP supporters.
Neither hospitals nor police were immediately available for comment.
The government has not acknowledged any deaths in the violence, although the Kompas daily on Wednesday quoted Hamid as saying 110 people had died in accidents during the campaign.
Hamid said 83 people had died in traffic accidents and 27 drowned when their boat sank on the way to a Golkar rally.
